title: The three-phase induction motor
oneLine: Three windings 120° apart make one field that turns at ns = 120f ÷ p; it cuts the shorted rotor bars and drags the rotor round, always a little slower, because with no slip nothing is cut and there is no torque.
skill: Explain the rotating field, slip and torque; work ns and slip from a nameplate (2950 rpm: two poles, 1.67%); know the starting current and torque, the light-load power factor, and the faults: single phasing, reversed rotation, insulation and winding balance.
specRefs: No syllabus yet: Dan's leading rate and Level 3 marine engineering syllabi to be mapped when he shares them (brief section 10)

title: The DOL starter
oneLine: Start makes the coil circuit, the coil pulls in the contactor, and the latch across Start keeps the coil fed; Stop or the overload's release contact drops it all out, and so does a power cut, so it never restarts by itself; full voltage at once means 6 to 8 times full-load current.
skill: Operate and fault-find a DOL starter from its drawing: the role of each part 1 to 10, no-volt protection, overload versus short-circuit protection, coil voltage; know the starting current and torque, why the supply sets the size limit, and what star-delta changes.
specRefs: No syllabus yet: Dan's leading rate and Level 3 marine engineering syllabi to be mapped when he shares them (brief section 10)
materialRefs: dol-study-sheet.jpg (Dan's own: parts 1-10, component list, four answered questions, uses and limits; item 7 and the inrush line corrected kindly, brief section 7)

title: The variable speed drive
oneLine: A VSD rectifies the supply to DC, smooths it and switches it back to AC at the frequency asked for; the field speed follows 120f ÷ p, and the voltage follows the frequency (8 V per Hz on a 400 V 50 Hz motor) so the flux stays the same up to base speed; on fans and pumps power falls with speed cubed.
skill: Explain rectifier, DC bus and inverter; set voltage from V/f for a given frequency; say what happens above base speed; estimate fan or pump power at reduced speed by the cube law and know when it does not apply; know the drive's usual trips and its limits.
specRefs: No syllabus yet: Dan's leading rate and Level 3 marine engineering syllabi to be mapped when he shares them (brief section 10)

title: The split-phase motor
oneLine: One phase alone makes a field that only pulses, so a second winding of thin wire at 90° carries a current that lags less, about 30° out of step, and the field turns; at about 75% speed the centrifugal switch drops the start winding out and the motor runs on the main winding.
skill: Explain why one winding cannot start a motor and how resistance makes the phase shift; know the low starting torque, the short-time-rated start winding, the switch's job, and the faults: hums but runs if spun, burnt start winding; reverse it by swapping the start winding's leads.
specRefs: No syllabus yet: Dan's leading rate and Level 3 marine engineering syllabi to be mapped when he shares them (brief section 10)

title: The capacitor-start motor
oneLine: A capacitor in series with the start winding makes its current lead, opening the angle between the two currents towards 90°; starting torque goes with the sine of that angle, so it roughly doubles over split-phase, and the switch still drops it out at 75 to 80% speed.
skill: Explain how the capacitor raises starting torque; compare split-phase, capacitor-start, capacitor-start capacitor-run and permanent split capacitor motors; recognise a failed start capacitor or switch and what to check.
specRefs: No syllabus yet: Dan's leading rate and Level 3 marine engineering syllabi to be mapped when he shares them (brief section 10)

title: The DC series motor
oneLine: One current runs through field and armature, so more load means more current, more field and torque rising with current squared (below saturation); a turning armature makes a back-emf, so at standstill only resistance limits the current, and with the load off the speed runs away.
skill: Explain back-emf and the starting current; explain torque against current squared and why the speed falls with load; know never to run it unloaded or on a belt, and why it has a starter and overspeed protection.
specRefs: No syllabus yet: Dan's leading rate and Level 3 marine engineering syllabi to be mapped when he shares them (brief section 10)

builds_on: AC circuits lesson 1 (a turning coil makes an emf)

title: The DC shunt motor
oneLine: The field sits across the supply, so its flux is steady; load it and the speed dips, the back-emf falls, more armature current flows and torque rises to match at a slightly lower speed; weaken the field and it runs faster, lose the field and it runs away.
skill: Use E = V − Ia Ra, speed ∝ E ÷ flux and torque ∝ flux × Ia to explain speed regulation and speed control by field and armature; know loss-of-field protection, starting at full field and the starter's no-volt coil.
specRefs: No syllabus yet: Dan's leading rate and Level 3 marine engineering syllabi to be mapped when he shares them (brief section 10)

title: The DC compound motor
oneLine: A series and a shunt field together: cumulative, they add, giving high starting torque with a speed that falls with load but stays safe unloaded; differential, they oppose and it is unstable, which is what a reversed series field gives you after a repair.
skill: Compare series, shunt and compound motors on starting torque, speed regulation and no-load behaviour; tell cumulative from differential and long from short shunt; diagnose a reversed series field.
